description: What outsiders get wrong, what the job actually consists of, and what it takes out of the person doing it. The myth questions are safe and fun; the personal-cost questions belong late in the episode and only with a guest who has warmed up.

questions.text: What do outsiders get most wrong about your work?
questions.lands_because: The most dependable question in the database. Every professional has this answer loaded and slightly irritated, and irritation makes for good audio.
followups: Where do you think that idea came from?

questions.text: What does the film or television version of your job get wrong?
questions.lands_because: Fun, low-stakes, and reliably specific. Also works as a warmup before the harder version - what the field gets wrong about itself.
followups: Is there one that gets it right?

questions.text: What does your own field tell the public about itself that is not quite true?
questions.lands_because: The hard version of the myth question, aimed inward instead of outward. Ask it right after the television version, while the guest is already in a debunking posture.
followups: Why does the field need that story?
questions.avoid_if: The guest holds a public-facing or communications role for their industry - they cannot answer it honestly and will resent being asked.

questions.text: What question do you get constantly that tells you the person does not understand your job?
questions.lands_because: Doubles as reconnaissance - it tells you exactly which questions to avoid for the rest of the interview, and guests appreciate being asked by someone who clearly does not want to be that person.
followups: What is the question they should be asking instead?

questions.text: What is a compliment you get that is not really a compliment?
questions.lands_because: Sharp and specific. 'You must be so patient', 'you must have a gift', 'it must be so rewarding' - each one carries a misconception the guest can unpack.
followups: What would an actual compliment be?

questions.text: What share of your time is the thing people think your job is?
questions.lands_because: Asking for a number forces precision, and the number is usually shockingly low. What fills the remainder is the actual subject of the episode.

questions.text: What is the unglamorous work that determines whether everything else succeeds?
questions.lands_because: Preparation, maintenance, documentation, and follow-through are the hidden load-bearing structure of every profession, and practitioners are gratified when someone asks about them.
followups: Does anyone measure or reward it?

questions.text: What is in your job that is not in your job description?
questions.lands_because: Catches the emotional labor, the mediation, the improvised social work that has crept into teaching, nursing, service, retail, and public-facing roles everywhere.
followups: When did that become part of the job?

setting_text.entrepreneur: What is in your work that you never expected to be doing when you started?

questions.text: What does this work cost you?
questions.lands_because: Direct, quiet, and unavoidable. Works only late, and works best when you then say nothing and let the pause run.
followups: Is it worth it? Ask yourself honestly.
questions.avoid_if: The guest has stayed formal throughout. A guarded guest will give you a platitude and you will have spent the question.

questions.text: Can a person do this job for thirty years? What happens to the ones who try?
questions.lands_because: The displacement onto 'the ones who try' lets the guest speak honestly about attrition, injury, and burnout without being asked to confess their own state.
followups: What do the ones who last do differently?

questions.text: How do you come down after a hard day?
questions.lands_because: Humane, easy, and it reveals the intensity of the work indirectly - the elaborateness of the ritual tells you what they are decompressing from.
followups: Did anyone teach you that, or did you work it out?

setting_text.entrepreneur: How do you come down after a hard day, with no commute to do it in?

questions.text: Would you want your kid to do this?
questions.lands_because: Compresses an entire assessment of a profession's future, dignity, and cost into one answer, and guests cannot give a talking point to it.
followups: What would you want them to know first?

questions.text: When did you last finish a day and feel genuinely good about it?
questions.lands_because: Ends on something true and positive without being saccharine, and the specificity of the answer often summarizes everything the guest values about the work.
